## Political views
Wu has stated the transgender movement's efforts to include transgender women in women's sports, which she considers an overreach, have unintentionally helped Republican anti-trans initiatives garner more political support.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-43) Wu claimed that "lunatic trans activists" were the "biggest obstacle to trans healthcare". She has also used transphobic slurs.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-44) In 2025, Wu apologized for suggesting that gender-affirming care to minors be restricted, writing, "Trans sisters, I was wrong. ... I genuinely thought that as a trans woman, if [I] ceded some points with the gender critical crowd we could have a healthier conversation and arrive at better public policy ... The problem is, they are getting crazier and more extreme... They are incapable of looking for a middle ground on bathrooms. They want maximalist policies on everything." Wu subsequently responded to a trans journalist who rejected Wu's apology by referring to her as "male-brained".[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-45)
texts.9:
## Personal life
In 2008, she married Frank Wu, four-time winner of the Hugo Award for Best Fan Artist. In 2020, she and Cenk Uygur co-founded Rebellion PAC, a political action committee with a focus on running advertisements in opposition to Donald Trump and in support of progressive get-out-the-vote efforts.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-46) She is a trans woman.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-48)
In October 2014, Wu posted multiple tweets about Gamergate advocates,[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-nyt-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-50) ridiculing them for "fighting an apocalyptic future where women are 8 percent of programmers and not 3 percent."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-GlobeFeature-5) While she was monitoring 8chan's pro-Gamergate chanboard (/gg/), anonymous users posted sensitive personal information about her, including at least one post containing her address. Subsequently, Wu began receiving multiple, specific rape and death threats including her address, causing Wu to flee her home.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-51) These threats have been widely attributed to Gamergate supporters.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-GlobeFeature-5)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-pbs-52) In December, Wu said that she had received emails that contained images of mutilated dogs from people who identified as Gamergate supporters, following the recent death of her dog.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-53)
texts.10:
## Personal life
Along with Anita Sarkeesian and Zoë Quinn, Wu was one of the targets of Gamergate harassment.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-nyt-49)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-pbs-52)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-time-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-55) In February 2015, she said, "by attacking me so viciously, they're helping give me the visibility to usher in the very game industry they're terrified about."[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-VentureBeat-56) Wu started a legal defense fund for women targeted by Gamergate. As of late 2014, the Wu family was also offering a cash reward for information leading to the prosecution of those who sent the death threats.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-59) By February 2015 she said she was spending a full day a week contacting law enforcement, and was only attending events in the US with a security detail.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-VentureBeat-56) In March 2015, she said she had received 48 death threats during the previous six months.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-60) As of May 2019, she and her husband were still living under aliases.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-Aliases-61)
texts.11:
## Personal life
In early 2017, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) closed its investigation of the matter. The FBI identified four men who sent threats and obtained confessions from two of them, one of whom stated that they had sent the threat as a "joke" but "understood that it was a federal crime to send a threatening communication to anyone and will never do it again". The U.S. Attorney for the District of Massachusetts declined to prosecute, giving no specific reason. Reacting to the report, Wu stated the FBI did not care about the investigation and that she was "livid".[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-BusInside-62) In the wake of the 2019 Poway synagogue shooting, however, she said that the FBI needs dedicated agents who understand online culture (8chan in particular).[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-8chan_and_radlicalization-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-The_Technology_202:_California_synagogue_shooting_puts_fringe_site_8chan_in_spotlight-64)
In August 2021, _The Washington Post_ reported that "despite the attempts to discredit her, wreck her career and destroy her sense of safety, Wu has now become a vocal proponent of forgiveness for those who apologize and show they have grown" but that "insults and continued harassment" still outnumbered apologies "10-to-1".[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-:0-65) Wu said that she was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder as a result of the harassment.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brianna_Wu#cite_note-:0-65)

Title: Harvard Business School on Instagram: "🎮 Founded in 2010, Supercell was a Finland-based mobile gaming company that had developed and launched five global hit mobile games: Clash of Clans, Clash Royale, Hay Day, Brawl Stars, and Boom Beach. The company’s early philosophy was that it could produce hits by designing the company with a structure and culture that would prove compelling to the industry’s top talent. Developers worked in small, autonomous groups called cells with little oversight. The formula was a success. Supercell had nearly $2 billion in annual revenues, and Clash of Clans alone had generated gross revenues of over $10 billion since inception. However, the company had not released a hit game in five years. 

In 2023, CEO Ilkka Paananen and the company’s leadership team decided to restructure the company into two divisions—New Games and Live Games. The New Game cells would retain the small team structures, which were largely flat and non-hierarchical, but the Live Game cells would add more traditional structure and hierarchy to exploit franchise hits. Now, Paananen wondered if Supercell could continue to attract top talent despite its shift to more traditional ways of managing the business. 

In the latest episode of Cold Call, Senior Lecturer Jeffrey Rayport and host Brian Kenny discuss the case, “Supercell 2.0: Clash of Plans,” and the question at its crux: What would it take to restore the company’s winning streak?

**Supercell Oy**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-5) is a Finnish mobile game development company based in Helsinki. Founded on 14 May 2010,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-6) the company's debut game was the browser game _Gunshine.net_, and after its release in 2011, Supercell started developing games for mobile devices. Since then, the company has fully released seven mobile games: _Hay Day_, _Clash of Clans_, _Boom Beach_, _Clash Royale_, _Brawl Stars_, _Squad Busters_ and _mo.co_, which are freemium games and have been very successful for the company, with an annual revenue of 2.65 billion euros as of 2026.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-7)
Following its rapid growth, Supercell opened additional offices in Shanghai, San Francisco, and Seoul. In 2016, the company was bought out by Chinese conglomerate Tencent holdings, taking an 81.4% stake in the company valued at €8.4 billion.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-8)

## Company
### Business model
Supercell focuses on the development of free-to-play games that yield profits through in-game microtransactions. The company's objective is to develop successful games that remain popular for years. The focus has not been on revenue, but on the principle "just design something great, something that users love".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-:0-9) Game development focuses on "cells" of five to seven people which start with an idea generation and an initial review by CEO Paananen.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-:0-9) The team subsequently develops the idea into a game, which the rest of the company's employees get to play-test, followed by play-testing in Canada's App Store; if the reception in Canada is good, the next step is global rollout (App Store).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-:0-9) Successful failures are celebrated by employees.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-:0-9) One of the games that was cancelled well into development was _Battle Buddies_, which had also been rated well in the test market, but the number of players was still too small. The final decision to cancel a project is made by the development team themselves.

## History
CEO and co-founder Ilkka Paananen in 2021

## History
### Background and founding
Before Supercell, two of its founders, Mikko Kodisoja and Ilkka Paananen, worked at Sumea, a mobile game company. Kodisoja co-founded Sumea in 1999, and Paananen was hired as the company's CEO in 2000. In 2003, Sumea made a profit of €1.2 million. In the following year, the American Digital Chocolate bought Sumea and made it the company's Finnish headquarters and Paananen the European manager. Kodisoja, the firm's creative director, left the company in 2010, followed soon after by Paananen.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-10)
Paananen moved to a venture capital company Lifeline Ventures, but wanted to create a game company where executives would not disturb the work of the game developers. Together, Paananen, Kodisoja, Petri Styrman, Lassi Leppinen, Visa Forstén, and Niko Derome, who had all known each other through work connections, founded Supercell in 2010. The company started its business in the Niittykumpu district of Espoo.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-lappalainen20152-11)

## History
### Background and founding
Kodisoja and Paananen invested €250,000 in the company. Tekes, the Finnish funding agency for technology innovation, loaned them a further €400,000 and Lifeline Ventures also invested in Supercell. The following October, Supercell raised €750,000 through seed funding, including from London Venture Partners and Initial Capital. The first game that Supercell started to develop was the massive multiplayer online game _Gunshine_ that could be played on Facebook with a browser or on mobile platforms. The game prototype was ready in eight months.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-lappalainen20152-11) After _Gunshine's_ completion, Accel Partners also invested €8 million in the company in May 2011, and shareholder Kevin Comolli became a member of Supercell's board of directors. Accel also invested in Rovio, among others.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-12)

## History
### Change of strategies
In November 2011, Supercell abandoned _Gunshine_ for three reasons: it did not interest players for long enough, it was too difficult to play, and the mobile version did not work as well as the browser version. At best, the game had approximately half a million players. Supercell considered Zynga's market leadership in games on the Facebook platform insurmountable and so decided to focus on iPad games, cancelling a Facebook game it was developing. In order to ease concerns of Supercell's investors due to the change of direction, Paananen increased the level of detail in progress reports.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-lappalainen20152-11)
The company simultaneously developed five games, and the first to be released for public testing was _Pets vs Orcs_. This game and _Tower_ were abandoned. In May 2012, _Hay Day_ was published and eventually became Supercell's first internationally released game.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-lappalainen20152-11)_Hay Day_ was Supercell's version of Zynga's successful Facebook game _FarmVille_, an easy-to-play farm simulator. Supercell added to their farming simulator the ability to refine products, a production chain, and touch-screen properties. The social aspect of the game was emphasised as well. In four months, the game became one of the most profitable games in Apple's App Store in the US, and was one of the most profitable in the world for two and a half years. The game received regular updates and was maintained by a team of 14 people.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-13)

🎮 Founded in 2010, Supercell was a Finland-based mobile gaming company that had developed and launched five global hit mobile games: Clash of Clans, Clash Royale, Hay Day, Brawl Stars, and Boom Beach. The company’s early philosophy was that it could produce hits by designing the company with a structure and culture that would prove compelling to the industry’s top talent. Developers worked in small, autonomous groups called cells with little oversight. The formula was a success. Supercell had nearly $2 billion in annual revenues, and Clash of Clans alone had generated gross revenues of over $10 billion since inception. However, the company had not released a hit game in five years.
In 2023, CEO Ilkka Paananen and the company’s leadership team decided to restructure the company into two divisions—New Games and Live Games. The New Game cells would retain the small team structures, which were largely flat and non-hierarchical, but the Live Game cells would add more traditional structure and hierarchy to exploit franchise hits. Now, Paananen wondered if Supercell could continue to attract top talent despite its shift to more traditional ways of managing the business.
In the latest episode of Cold Call, Senior Lecturer Jeffrey Rayport and host Brian Kenny discuss the case, “Supercell 2.0: Clash of Plans,” and the question at its crux: What would it take to restore the company’s winning streak?

texts.1:
**Supercell Oy**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-5) is a Finnish mobile game development company based in Helsinki. Founded on 14 May 2010,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-6) the company's debut game was the browser game _Gunshine.net_, and after its release in 2011, Supercell started developing games for mobile devices. Since then, the company has fully released seven mobile games: _Hay Day_, _Clash of Clans_, _Boom Beach_, _Clash Royale_, _Brawl Stars_, _Squad Busters_ and _mo.co_, which are freemium games and have been very successful for the company, with an annual revenue of 2.65 billion euros as of 2026.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-7)
Following its rapid growth, Supercell opened additional offices in Shanghai, San Francisco, and Seoul. In 2016, the company was bought out by Chinese conglomerate Tencent holdings, taking an 81.4% stake in the company valued at €8.4 billion.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-8)
texts.2:
## Company
### Business model
Supercell focuses on the development of free-to-play games that yield profits through in-game microtransactions. The company's objective is to develop successful games that remain popular for years. The focus has not been on revenue, but on the principle "just design something great, something that users love".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-:0-9) Game development focuses on "cells" of five to seven people which start with an idea generation and an initial review by CEO Paananen.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-:0-9) The team subsequently develops the idea into a game, which the rest of the company's employees get to play-test, followed by play-testing in Canada's App Store; if the reception in Canada is good, the next step is global rollout (App Store).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-:0-9) Successful failures are celebrated by employees.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-:0-9) One of the games that was cancelled well into development was _Battle Buddies_, which had also been rated well in the test market, but the number of players was still too small. The final decision to cancel a project is made by the development team themselves.
texts.3:
## History
CEO and co-founder Ilkka Paananen in 2021
texts.4:
## History
### Background and founding
Before Supercell, two of its founders, Mikko Kodisoja and Ilkka Paananen, worked at Sumea, a mobile game company. Kodisoja co-founded Sumea in 1999, and Paananen was hired as the company's CEO in 2000. In 2003, Sumea made a profit of €1.2 million. In the following year, the American Digital Chocolate bought Sumea and made it the company's Finnish headquarters and Paananen the European manager. Kodisoja, the firm's creative director, left the company in 2010, followed soon after by Paananen.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-10)
Paananen moved to a venture capital company Lifeline Ventures, but wanted to create a game company where executives would not disturb the work of the game developers. Together, Paananen, Kodisoja, Petri Styrman, Lassi Leppinen, Visa Forstén, and Niko Derome, who had all known each other through work connections, founded Supercell in 2010. The company started its business in the Niittykumpu district of Espoo.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-lappalainen20152-11)
texts.5:
## History
### Background and founding
Kodisoja and Paananen invested €250,000 in the company. Tekes, the Finnish funding agency for technology innovation, loaned them a further €400,000 and Lifeline Ventures also invested in Supercell. The following October, Supercell raised €750,000 through seed funding, including from London Venture Partners and Initial Capital. The first game that Supercell started to develop was the massive multiplayer online game _Gunshine_ that could be played on Facebook with a browser or on mobile platforms. The game prototype was ready in eight months.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-lappalainen20152-11) After _Gunshine's_ completion, Accel Partners also invested €8 million in the company in May 2011, and shareholder Kevin Comolli became a member of Supercell's board of directors. Accel also invested in Rovio, among others.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-12)
texts.6:
## History
### Change of strategies
In November 2011, Supercell abandoned _Gunshine_ for three reasons: it did not interest players for long enough, it was too difficult to play, and the mobile version did not work as well as the browser version. At best, the game had approximately half a million players. Supercell considered Zynga's market leadership in games on the Facebook platform insurmountable and so decided to focus on iPad games, cancelling a Facebook game it was developing. In order to ease concerns of Supercell's investors due to the change of direction, Paananen increased the level of detail in progress reports.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-lappalainen20152-11)
The company simultaneously developed five games, and the first to be released for public testing was _Pets vs Orcs_. This game and _Tower_ were abandoned. In May 2012, _Hay Day_ was published and eventually became Supercell's first internationally released game.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-lappalainen20152-11)_Hay Day_ was Supercell's version of Zynga's successful Facebook game _FarmVille_, an easy-to-play farm simulator. Supercell added to their farming simulator the ability to refine products, a production chain, and touch-screen properties. The social aspect of the game was emphasised as well. In four months, the game became one of the most profitable games in Apple's App Store in the US, and was one of the most profitable in the world for two and a half years. The game received regular updates and was maintained by a team of 14 people.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell_(company)#cite_note-13)

**THQ Inc.** was an American video game company based in Agoura Hills, California. It was founded in April 1990 by Jack Friedman, originally in Calabasas, and became a public company the following year through a reverse merger takeover. Initially working in the toy business, it expanded into the video game business through several acquisitions before shifting its focus away from toys entirely. THQ continued its trend of acquiring companies throughout the 2000s.

The company published both internally created and externally licensed content in its product portfolio. THQ's internally created game series included _Darksiders_, _De Blob_, _Destroy All Humans!_, _MX vs. ATV_, _Red Faction_, and _Saints Row_, among others. The company also held exclusive, long-term licensing agreements with sports and entertainment content creators, such as Disney/Pixar, DreamWorks Animation, Nickelodeon, and WWE.
After years of financial struggles, stock value drop, and debt, THQ filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in December 2012 and commenced liquidation of its assets the following month. Several properties were auctioned to other companies, while the remaining staff were laid off. The "THQ" trademark was eventually acquired by developer Nordic Games (which had also acquired some of THQ's auctioned-off properties) in 2014 and assumed the name "THQ Nordic" in 2016, while continuing a variety of its franchises under said name.

### Background and foundation (1990–1999)
[edit]
Former logo, used from 2000 to 2011
THQ Inc. was founded by LJN co-founder Jack Friedman in April 1990.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-LA_Times_1991-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-Founding-2) "THQ" is an initialism for "Toy Headquarters".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-LA_Times_1991-1) THQ acquired New Ventures, a division of Broderbund, in September 1990.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-3) In 1991, Trinity Acquisition Corp, a NASDAQ-listed special-purpose acquisition company (SPAC), agreed to acquire and merge with THQ in a reverse merger takeover.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-LA_Times_1991-1) The deal was a stock swap valued at about $33 million, with THQ's shareholders owning 51.7% of the new entity.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-4) THQ's name was retained for the new company, its ticker symbol was changed to "THQI", and Friedman was named as its president.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-LA_Times_1991-1)
In 1992, THQ and Nickelodeon decided to begin their relationship with their line of video games based on the television show _The Ren & Stimpy Show_ for Nintendo game consoles.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-6)

### Background and foundation (1990–1999)
THQ then acquired video game developer Black Pearl Software of Chicago in 1993.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-7) Following the acquisition, THQ would use the Black Pearl Software name for its Sega games, while the Malibu Games name would be used for the Nintendo games. In mid 1993, the company partnered with Malibu Comics to develop video games based on the Ultraforce, but never came to fruition, with one of these instead went to Sony Imagesoft.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-8)
THQ withdrew completely from the toy business in 1994 to focus solely on video game production.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-THQ_history-9) Around the same time, the company entered into a deal with Electronic Arts to license five titles for various consoles.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-10) Jack Friedman then left the company in 1995 to co-found the toy manufacturer Jakks Pacific.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-11)
At the Winter CES 1995, THQ signed an expanded deal with Electronic Arts to develop games for its 16-bit and 8-bit home consoles and handheld titles.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-12) From then on, the Black Pearl Software name would be used for 8-bit and 16-bit games, while THQ introduced the Kokopeli Digital Studios brand name for its 32-bit games.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-13)

# Rodger Saffold plays 'poor man's Stan Kroenke' to rising esports powerhouse
Tennessee Titans lineman Rodger Saffold, center, saw his Rise Nation squad soar to success during the Call of Duty World League season in 2018. The team, which missed out on Call of Duty League franchising, will get a new look soon.MLG
*    Lindsey ThiryJul 9, 2018, 07:45 AM ET
Multiple Authors
Share
*   Copy Link  
*   [Email](mailto:?subject=Rodger%20Saffold%20plays%20%27poor%20man%27s%20Stan%20Kroenke%27%20to%20rising%20esports%20powerhouse&body=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.espn.com%2Fblog%2Flos%2Dangeles%2Drams%2Fpost%2F_%2Fid%2F38624)  
*   Print
ANAHEIM, Calif. -- A rainbow of strobe lights dances across the championship banners that line a walkway leading from an ordinary, brightly lit convention center lobby to a dark arena that feels like an alternate universe.
Dramatic theme music fills the air, as smoke from a machine dissipates to reveal a gamer’s heaven.
Oversized monitors in the rafters broadcast the action, and speakers boom with an intense amount of bass.
Then, a team delivers a final kill shot, and a crowd of several thousand erupts in cheers.

# Rodger Saffold plays 'poor man's Stan Kroenke' to rising esports powerhouse
## Best of NFL Nation
• How are teams countering the 'Peanut Punch'?
• Justin Jefferson's legendary one-handed grab
• Burrow, Bengals soaring into division duel
In the middle of this scene at the Call of Duty World League tournament is Los Angeles Rams offensive guard Rodger Saffold. He finished mandatory minicamp only the week prior, and he’s tending to his other job as owner of Rise Nation, an esports team that he founded in 2014, which boasts several of the top video game players and teams in the country.
“The lights are crazy; the energy is amazing,” said Saffold, who, at 6-foot-5 and 325 pounds, stood out among the crowd, wearing a black sweatshirt and a diamond-encrusted pendant with a Rise Nation logo. “It’s also very stressful.”
For six months a year, Saffold is strictly focused on football. But when the season ends, the nine-year NFL pro fills much of his time with gaming. He grew up loving puzzles. Then during college, he developed a penchant for video games, more specifically “Call of Duty,” the first-person-shooter game.
“I was streaming my [video game] play on Twitch,” Saffold said, referring to a live-streaming video platform. “Somebody gave me the idea that we should probably just come up with our own team, and I decided to make it from scratch.”
The structure of an esports organization bears a resemblance to an NFL team.
As the owner, Saffold funds the organization, “like a poor man’s Stan Kroenke,” he chuckled, in reference to the Rams’ owner. He has a partner in longtime friend Kareem Horsley and hired former gamer Jonathan Tucker as general manager.
“In big decisions, we keep him informed,” said Tucker, who first met Saffold in 2014 at a gaming tournament. “Transfers, signings, big-money moves that could affect how we work, we have to consult him. ... But as far as day-to-day stuff, me and Kareem do most of it, because it’s just too many things to bother him with.”

# Rodger Saffold plays 'poor man's Stan Kroenke' to rising esports powerhouse
## Best of NFL Nation
Saffold, who studied business management at Indiana, has 10 full-time employees and a roster that fluctuates between 10 and 12 players among seven teams, depending on the games and tournaments the organization is involved in.
To develop his business, Saffold leaned on the friendships he developed within the esports industry. “Just picking everybody’s brain,” Saffold said, “we were kind of able to figure out a formula.”
He also sought the creative input of a Rams graphic designer to develop a Rise Nation logo.
“I wanted to be involved and invested into something that I have a lot of passion for,” Saffold said. “This seemed to be it.”
Saffold isn’t the only person from professional sports getting into gaming. Earlier this year, the NBA became the first professional sports league to operate an esports league when it launched NBA 2K, which features some of the best basketball gamers in the world.
Magic Johnson, Shaquille O’Neal, Rick Fox, Alex Rodriguez and Jimmy Rollins are among former athletes who have invested in esports.
But Saffold is one of only two current professional athlete to own an organization, something he takes pride in.
“I’m making money at it,” Saffold said. “But at the same time, I started off with ‘Call of Duty’ and now I’ve ventured into different games and different sports, and we kind of developed a nice community of people surrounded by Rise that just enjoy the organization that we created.”
His gamer tag is Rise Blindside, and, during the offseason, Saffold can often be found huddled in front of three screens inside his game room at home, competing against friends and Rise Nation players.
“He is so supportive and so engaged,” said Daniel Loza, a member of Rise Nation’s Call of Duty team. “It’s not just a business thing, like you play for me. He gets to know you, know what you like. ... I’ve played [Call of Duty] before with him. I’ve played games with him. ... He’s a gamer, so he understands.”
At the Call of Duty World League tournament in Anaheim, fans in Rise Nation jerseys stopped Saffold for photos and autographs.

# Rodger Saffold plays 'poor man's Stan Kroenke' to rising esports powerhouse
## Best of NFL Nation
“At first they’re like, ‘Oh man, there goes the Rise Nation owner,’” Saffold said. “Then they’re like ‘Oh, it’s a Rams football player.’ ... So I’ve had autographs for my gamer tag as well as for football.”
But when his team took the controls, Saffold became all but unapproachable. His eyes were fixated on the screen as he hardly blinked.
Saffold's Rise Nation team in action.MLG
“This is about to get serious!” he said to no one in particular, when his team heated up after a slow start. “This is going to be close. Wow, that shot was ridiculous. ... Let’s go!”
The running commentary continued until his team completed a come-from-behind win in the first game and swept the match. Following the victory, he quietly made his way to another screen to scout future opponents. Even during a meal break, Saffold clutched his phone to watch the action online.
“Before I got started with this, I was a fan,” Saffold said. “I wasn’t a corporation trying to just get into esports. ... So being able to come to these things and just watch game play, because as a gamer, I watch these guys, and I’m picking up tips.”
Tucker said it was rare to see an owner as involved as Saffold.
“He likes games,” Tucker said. “So it’s a lot different to come sit around all day with everybody.”
The four-member Rise Nation Call of Duty team has won three tournaments this season, including its most recent in Anaheim, where it took home $80,000 of a $200,000 prize pool.
Rise Nation's team is the favorite going into the Call of Duty World League Championship in Columbus, Ohio, in August, where the prize pool will increase to $1.5 million.
“Definitely want that world championship for Call of Duty,” Saffold said. “It puts us at another notch and just that premier level. ... We’ve got a pretty decent following, but I think grabbing a world championship would take us over the top.”
And other Rams want to get involved.

# Rodger Saffold plays 'poor man's Stan Kroenke' to rising esports powerhouse
## Best of NFL Nation
Saffold won’t reveal any names. He’s not ready to expand the business yet and doesn’t want to tip other teams to potential investors or owners when they could one day help him grow Rise Nation.
“At first we were thinking this was more of a hobby,” Saffold said. “But now it has kind of grown, and having more than one team and having players from all over the world has really been shocking thus far. We’re only five years into this.”

**THQ Inc.** was an American video game company based in Agoura Hills, California. It was founded in April 1990 by Jack Friedman, originally in Calabasas, and became a public company the following year through a reverse merger takeover. Initially working in the toy business, it expanded into the video game business through several acquisitions before shifting its focus away from toys entirely. THQ continued its trend of acquiring companies throughout the 2000s.
texts.1:
The company published both internally created and externally licensed content in its product portfolio. THQ's internally created game series included _Darksiders_, _De Blob_, _Destroy All Humans!_, _MX vs. ATV_, _Red Faction_, and _Saints Row_, among others. The company also held exclusive, long-term licensing agreements with sports and entertainment content creators, such as Disney/Pixar, DreamWorks Animation, Nickelodeon, and WWE.
After years of financial struggles, stock value drop, and debt, THQ filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in December 2012 and commenced liquidation of its assets the following month. Several properties were auctioned to other companies, while the remaining staff were laid off. The "THQ" trademark was eventually acquired by developer Nordic Games (which had also acquired some of THQ's auctioned-off properties) in 2014 and assumed the name "THQ Nordic" in 2016, while continuing a variety of its franchises under said name.

### Background and foundation (1990–1999)

THQ Inc. was founded by LJN co-founder Jack Friedman in April 1990.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-LA_Times_1991-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-Founding-2) "THQ" is an initialism for "Toy Headquarters".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-LA_Times_1991-1) THQ acquired New Ventures, a division of Broderbund, in September 1990.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-3) In 1991, Trinity Acquisition Corp, a NASDAQ-listed special-purpose acquisition company (SPAC), agreed to acquire and merge with THQ in a reverse merger takeover.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-LA_Times_1991-1) The deal was a stock swap valued at about $33 million, with THQ's shareholders owning 51.7% of the new entity.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-4) THQ's name was retained for the new company, its ticker symbol was changed to "THQI", and Friedman was named as its president.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-LA_Times_1991-1)
In 1992, THQ and Nickelodeon decided to begin their relationship with their line of video games based on the television show _The Ren & Stimpy Show_ for Nintendo game consoles.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-6)

THQ then acquired video game developer Black Pearl Software of Chicago in 1993.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-7) Following the acquisition, THQ would use the Black Pearl Software name for its Sega games, while the Malibu Games name would be used for the Nintendo games. In mid 1993, the company partnered with Malibu Comics to develop video games based on the Ultraforce, but never came to fruition, with one of these instead went to Sony Imagesoft.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-8)
THQ withdrew completely from the toy business in 1994 to focus solely on video game production.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-THQ_history-9) Around the same time, the company entered into a deal with Electronic Arts to license five titles for various consoles.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-10) Jack Friedman then left the company in 1995 to co-found the toy manufacturer Jakks Pacific.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-11)
At the Winter CES 1995, THQ signed an expanded deal with Electronic Arts to develop games for its 16-bit and 8-bit home consoles and handheld titles.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-12) From then on, the Black Pearl Software name would be used for 8-bit and 16-bit games, while THQ introduced the Kokopeli Digital Studios brand name for its 32-bit games.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THQ#cite_note-13)

Title: Anna Kournikova’s Father Denied Secret Wedding Rumors—Then NHL Star Sergei Fedorov Said They Were Married
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4
Sergei Fedorov gave a blunt answer when asked about rumors that he had married Anna Kournikova. "They are true. We were married, albeit brief, and we are now divorced," he told The Hockey News in its March 14, 2003 issue.
The Detroit Red Wings star was 33 and Kournikova was 21 when the interview appeared. He said their age difference helped explain the public fascination with them and that he was no longer in contact with her.
Her father, Sergei Kournikov, had already complained about persistent questions concerning his daughter's personal life. The coverage had shifted between Fedorov and another Russian NHL star, Florida Panthers player Pavel Bure.
Kournikova had begun dating Enrique Iglesias by the time Fedorov spoke publicly. The former tennis player and Spanish singer have since built a family together while sharing relatively little about their relationship.

## Her Father Denied Reports of a Secret Wedding in Moscow
In July 2001, Britain's _The Sun_ reported that Kournikova and Fedorov had married in Moscow during Wimbledon. It attributed a statement to Fedorov's mother, Natalya, describing a lovely ceremony and her happiness at becoming Kournikova's mother-in-law.
Kournikov rejected the story in a telephone interview with Reuters. According to ABC News, he said his daughter was training in Florida and had not been in Moscow since the Kremlin Cup the previous November.
He also questioned the statement attributed to Natalya, saying he understood that she lived in Detroit. His account directly challenged the tabloid's description of the supposed ceremony.
Fedorov's later interview did not provide wedding or divorce dates or identify where a ceremony had taken place.

## Pavel Bure's Reported Proposal Was Followed by an Engagement Denial
A separate story had circulated in 2000, when witnesses said Bure proposed to Kournikova at The Forge restaurant in Miami Beach. An Associated Press report described photographs of them together and the restaurant owner's account of toasting an engagement.
The athletes initially gave reporters little clarity. Asked whether the news was true, Bure answered, "Maybe, yeah," while Kournikova said she had no details to share.
Kournikova subsequently denied being engaged or planning to marry. Bure said a wedding was not in his immediate plans, CBS News reported.
Fedorov later addressed the Bure coverage in his 2003 interview. He said he had read about it in magazines and tried to end his relationship with Kournikova, but accepted her explanation and reconciled with her. He did not offer a clear account of what had happened between her and Bure.

## Kournikova Met Enrique Iglesias on the Set of 'Escape'
Video 3  
Kournikova appeared as Iglesias' love interest in the video for "Escape," filmed in 2001. Their onscreen pairing led to a relationship away from the cameras.
In an October 2023 interview with PEOPLE, Iglesias said their different careers came with a shared understanding of fame. She knew what his world involved, and he understood the attention surrounding hers.
He described their connection as something that strengthened gradually. He also spoke about learning along the way and getting through difficult periods together.

## The Couple Now Shares Four Children
Kournikova and Iglesias welcomed twins Lucy and Nicolas in December 2017, followed by daughter Mary in January 2020. Their youngest son, Romeo, was born on December 17, 2025.
In his 2023 interview, Iglesias described his older children as enthusiastic listeners to his music. When a difficult school pickup turned into tears or arguments, asking for a favorite song could get them singing "I Like It" together.
Kournikova revealed Romeo's name on March 19, 2026, with a photograph of all four children together on a boat. Her caption listed their names: "Lucy+Nicolas+Mary+Romeo," followed by four red hearts.

The question _is Shigeru Miyamoto married?_ has lingered in gaming circles for decades, a whisper among fans who trace the origins of their favorite franchises back to the man who shaped them. Miyamoto, Nintendo’s legendary designer behind _Super Mario_, _The Legend of Zelda_, and _Donkey Kong_, has spent his career crafting worlds where love stories unfold—yet his own romantic life has remained deliberately obscured. Speculation flares up every time he appears at an event with a woman on his arm, or when interviews touch on family, only to be met with polite deflection. The ambiguity isn’t accidental; it’s a testament to how Miyamoto, now in his late 60s, has mastered the art of balancing public adoration with private boundaries. What’s striking isn’t just the lack of clarity, but the _why_ behind it. In an industry where executives and celebrities often court media attention, Miyamoto’s reticence stands out. Yet the truth, as with many aspects of his life, lies in the details: the glimpses of companionship, the professional partnerships, and the cultural context that shapes how a man of his standing navigates privacy. The confusion isn’t just about Miyamoto’s personal life, but about the expectations placed on creative icons. Game developers like Miyamoto occupy a unique space: they’re both artists and corporate figures, their work intertwined with their identities. When a designer’s life becomes public fodder, it risks overshadowing their contributions. Miyamoto’s approach—keeping his relationships out of the spotlight—reflects a broader trend among Japanese professionals in creative fields, where personal and professional spheres often remain distinct. But in an era where even minor details of celebrities’ lives are dissected, the question _is Shigeru Miyamoto married?_ persists, revealing as much about fans’ curiosity as it does about the man himself.

## Common Myths About Shigeru Miyamoto’s Personal Life
The most enduring myth surrounding Miyamoto is that his marital status is a closely guarded secret because he’s never been married at all. This assumption stems from the scarcity of public statements and the absence of a high-profile partner in interviews or events. Yet the idea that a man who’s spent decades designing games about love and companionship—from _Mario_’s courtship of Peach to _Zelda_’s romantic subplots—would remain single is more about fan projection than reality. The truth is simpler: Miyamoto has never confirmed or denied marriage, but the evidence suggests otherwise. Another persistent myth is that Miyamoto’s marriage, if it exists, is a product of corporate necessity—a strategic union to solidify his legacy or appease Nintendo’s traditionalist shareholders. ## Common Myths About Shigeru Miyamoto’s Personal Life
### Myth 1: Shigeru Miyamoto Has Never Been Married
The claim that Miyamoto is unmarried is the most tenacious, fueled by decades of silence and the lack of a visible partner in public appearances. Yet this myth ignores the cultural norms of discretion, particularly in Japan, where even well-known figures often keep their personal lives private. Miyamoto’s occasional references to "my family" in Japanese interviews—such as his 2015 remarks about balancing work and time with loved ones—suggest that he does have a partner or children, though he never specifies. ### Myth 2: His Marriage Is a Corporate Strategy
The idea that Miyamoto’s marital status is a calculated move by Nintendo to enhance his image is a product of Western media’s tendency to interpret Japanese professionalism through a transactional lens. Sergei Fedorov gave a blunt answer when asked about rumors that he had married Anna Kournikova. "They are true. We were married, albeit brief, and we are now divorced," he told The Hockey News in its March 14, 2003 issue.
The Detroit Red Wings star was 33 and Kournikova was 21 when the interview appeared. He said their age difference helped explain the public fascination with them and that he was no longer in contact with her.
Her father, Sergei Kournikov, had already complained about persistent questions concerning his daughter's personal life. The coverage had shifted between Fedorov and another Russian NHL star, Florida Panthers player Pavel Bure.
Kournikova had begun dating Enrique Iglesias by the time Fedorov spoke publicly. The former tennis player and Spanish singer have since built a family together while sharing relatively little about their relationship.
texts.1:
## Her Father Denied Reports of a Secret Wedding in Moscow
In July 2001, Britain's _The Sun_ reported that Kournikova and Fedorov had married in Moscow during Wimbledon. It attributed a statement to Fedorov's mother, Natalya, describing a lovely ceremony and her happiness at becoming Kournikova's mother-in-law.
Kournikov rejected the story in a telephone interview with Reuters. According to ABC News, he said his daughter was training in Florida and had not been in Moscow since the Kremlin Cup the previous November.
He also questioned the statement attributed to Natalya, saying he understood that she lived in Detroit. His account directly challenged the tabloid's description of the supposed ceremony.
Fedorov's later interview did not provide wedding or divorce dates or identify where a ceremony had taken place.
texts.2:
## Pavel Bure's Reported Proposal Was Followed by an Engagement Denial
A separate story had circulated in 2000, when witnesses said Bure proposed to Kournikova at The Forge restaurant in Miami Beach. An Associated Press report described photographs of them together and the restaurant owner's account of toasting an engagement.
The athletes initially gave reporters little clarity. Asked whether the news was true, Bure answered, "Maybe, yeah," while Kournikova said she had no details to share.
Kournikova subsequently denied being engaged or planning to marry. Bure said a wedding was not in his immediate plans, CBS News reported.
Fedorov later addressed the Bure coverage in his 2003 interview. He said he had read about it in magazines and tried to end his relationship with Kournikova, but accepted her explanation and reconciled with her. He did not offer a clear account of what had happened between her and Bure.
texts.3:
## Kournikova Met Enrique Iglesias on the Set of 'Escape'
Video 3  
Kournikova appeared as Iglesias' love interest in the video for "Escape," filmed in 2001. Their onscreen pairing led to a relationship away from the cameras.
In an October 2023 interview with PEOPLE, Iglesias said their different careers came with a shared understanding of fame. She knew what his world involved, and he understood the attention surrounding hers.
He described their connection as something that strengthened gradually. He also spoke about learning along the way and getting through difficult periods together.
texts.4:
## The Couple Now Shares Four Children
Kournikova and Iglesias welcomed twins Lucy and Nicolas in December 2017, followed by daughter Mary in January 2020. Their youngest son, Romeo, was born on December 17, 2025.
In his 2023 interview, Iglesias described his older children as enthusiastic listeners to his music. When a difficult school pickup turned into tears or arguments, asking for a favorite song could get them singing "I Like It" together.
Kournikova revealed Romeo's name on March 19, 2026, with a photograph of all four children together on a boat. Her caption listed their names: "Lucy+Nicolas+Mary+Romeo," followed by four red hearts.
